about: Justification trainer prompts for Unit 3, Cellular Energetics (docs/apbio-architecture.md, "Justification trainer").

prompts.title: A saliva enzyme at stomach pH
prompts.context:
Amylase from saliva breaks starch into smaller sugars. Students measured its activity at 37 °C at several pH values, as a percent of its highest activity.

pHActivity (% of maximum)
415
548
692
7100
871
prompts.prompt: Predict the rate of starch breakdown by this enzyme at pH 2, and justify your prediction with a mechanism.
checklist: Predicts activity near zero at pH 2, lower than the 15% measured at pH 4
Uses the trend: activity falls from 100% at pH 7 to 15% at pH 4 as pH drops
Says the high H+ concentration changes the charges on R groups, breaking ionic and hydrogen bonds that hold the enzyme's shape
Says the active site changes shape, so starch fits poorly and few enzyme-substrate complexes form

earns.answer: The rate at pH 2 will be close to zero, lower than the 15% measured at pH 4. Activity drops steadily as pH falls below 7: 92% at pH 6, 48% at pH 5 and 15% at pH 4. At pH 2 the H+ concentration is 100 times higher than at pH 4. The extra H+ ions bind to R groups that are normally negatively charged, which changes their charges. Ionic bonds and hydrogen bonds between R groups break, so the enzyme's tertiary structure and its active site change shape. Starch no longer fits the active site well, so few enzyme-substrate complexes form and little starch is broken down.
earns.why: The prediction follows the data, and the justification is a chain from H+ to R group charges to active site shape to rate.

misses.answer: The rate will be lower because the acid at pH 2 denatures the enzyme.
misses.why: The direction is right, but it uses no data and "denatures" names the outcome without saying how H+ changes R groups and the active site.

prompts.title: Where does inhibitor X bind?
prompts.context:
Researchers measured the rate of an enzyme reaction at four substrate concentrations, with and without a fixed amount of inhibitor X.

Substrate (mM)Rate, no inhibitor (µmol/min)Rate, with X (µmol/min)
1104
53016
204434
804947

A student claims that X binds to the enzyme's active site.
prompts.prompt: Support or refute the student's claim using evidence from the table and reasoning about how inhibitors work.
checklist: Supports the claim, citing low substrate evidence: at 1 mM the rate falls from 10 to 4 µmol/min with X, 60% lower
Cites high substrate evidence: at 80 mM the rate is 47 versus 49 µmol/min, only about 4% lower
Reasons that X and substrate compete for the active site, so at high substrate most active sites hold substrate and few bind X
Says an inhibitor that bound elsewhere and changed the enzyme's shape would still lower the rate at high substrate

earns.answer: The data support the claim. At 1 mM substrate, X lowers the rate from 10 to 4 µmol/min, a 60% drop. At 80 mM substrate, the rate with X is 47 µmol/min compared with 49 µmol/min without it, only about 4% lower. So adding more substrate almost cancels the effect of X. This fits a competitive inhibitor: X and the substrate compete for the same active site. At high substrate concentration, substrate molecules occupy most active sites, so X binds few enzymes. An inhibitor that bound somewhere else and changed the enzyme's shape would still lower the rate at high substrate, because extra substrate could not undo that change.
earns.why: It takes a side, uses values at both ends of the range, and explains why the pattern points to the active site and not to another site.

misses.answer: The claim is supported because X lowers the reaction rate at every substrate concentration.
misses.why: Any inhibitor lowers the rate. The evidence that matters is that high substrate almost removes the effect, and the answer gives no reasoning about competition.

prompts.title: Net oxygen output across light levels
prompts.context:
A student measured net oxygen production by a water plant at 25 °C under six light intensities. Net production is oxygen released by photosynthesis minus oxygen used by cellular respiration.

Light intensity (µmol photons/m²/s)Net O2 production (mL/h)
0−0.4
1000.8
2001.9
4003.2
8003.4
16003.4
prompts.prompt: Describe how net oxygen production changes with light intensity, using values from the table, and explain the value at 0 light and why production levels off at high light.
checklist: From 0 to 400 µmol photons/m²/s, net O2 production rises from −0.4 to 3.2 mL/h
Above 400, it levels off: 3.2 mL/h at 400 and 3.4 mL/h at both 800 and 1600
At 0 light the value is negative because the plant still uses O2 in cellular respiration while no photosynthesis occurs
Gives a reason for the leveling off: something other than light, such as CO2 supply or Calvin cycle enzymes, limits the rate

earns.answer: Net oxygen production rises with light intensity at first, then levels off. It goes from −0.4 mL/h at 0 light to 0.8 mL/h at 100, 1.9 mL/h at 200 and 3.2 mL/h at 400 µmol photons/m²/s. Above 400 it barely changes: 3.4 mL/h at both 800 and 1600. At high light, another factor such as the CO2 supply or the speed of the Calvin cycle limits the rate. At 0 light the value is negative because the plant still uses oxygen in cellular respiration, but no photosynthesis releases oxygen, so it takes up 0.4 mL of O2 each hour.
earns.why: It describes both parts of the curve with values and units, and explains the negative value with respiration and the plateau with another limit.

misses.answer: Oxygen production goes up as light intensity goes up, because more light means more photosynthesis.
misses.why: It gives no values, misses the plateau above 400 and does not explain why the value at 0 light is negative.

prompts.title: A leak in the inner membrane
prompts.context:
Model: in the inner mitochondrial membrane, electrons from NADH pass along the electron transport chain to O2. As electrons pass, chain proteins pump H+ from the matrix into the intermembrane space. H+ flows back into the matrix through ATP synthase, and this flow drives ATP synthesis.

A compound lets H+ cross the inner membrane directly. In isolated mitochondria, adding the compound raised O2 use from 2.0 to 3.6 nmol/min per mg protein, while ATP production fell from 5.0 to 0.8 nmol/min per mg protein.
prompts.prompt: Use the model to explain why the compound lowers ATP production even though the mitochondria keep using O2.
checklist: Says electron transport to O2 still runs, so O2 is still used as the final electron acceptor
Says H+ pumped into the intermembrane space returns through the compound instead of through ATP synthase, so the H+ gradient is smaller
Says ATP synthase makes ATP only when H+ flows through it, so less flow through ATP synthase means less ATP (5.0 down to 0.8)

earns.answer: In the model, electrons from NADH pass along the electron transport chain to O2, the final electron acceptor. As they pass, the chain pumps H+ from the matrix into the intermembrane space, building a high H+ concentration there. Normally H+ flows back through ATP synthase, and that flow drives ATP synthesis. The compound gives H+ another path across the inner membrane. Electron transport still runs, so O2 is still used, but most H+ returns through the compound instead of ATP synthase. The H+ gradient becomes smaller and less H+ flows through ATP synthase, so ATP production falls from 5.0 to 0.8 nmol/min per mg protein.
earns.why: It uses each step of the model to separate electron transport (which uses O2) from ATP synthesis (which needs H+ flow through ATP synthase).

misses.answer: The compound stops the electron transport chain, so less ATP is made.
misses.why: It contradicts the data, since O2 use continued. It misses that the compound lets H+ bypass ATP synthase.
